catalog_quote: 2.4 Stress. Stress is predictable in Neve‘ei with the primary stress falling on the penultimate syllable as shown in (2.46) where the last two syllables contain single vowels. (2.46) /ˈvenox/ ‘steal’ /meˈtabux/ ‘morning’ /ˈmoxot/ ‘torn, ripped’ /ˈnowi/ ‘water’. In the examples in (2.47), when a word ends in a sequence of -VV(C), the stress falls on the first of the two vowels. (2.47) /nesaˈxau/ ‘year, age’ /naˈʔai/ ‘tree’ /luˈxei/ ‘go over, step over’ /noˈxoim/ ‘Pacific pigeon’ /ɡiˈlou/ ‘look, open one’s eyes, wake up’. When a single syllable suffix is added to a word, the stress moves to the right in order to fall on the penultimate syllable. (2.48) /ˈnebat-n/ ‘leg-3SGPOSS’ /neˈbat-uŋ/ ‘leg-1SGPOSS’. ... [2.3.1] It is also possible for a syllable to contain two vowels in sequence, but as such sequences are encountered only in restricted environments, they are described separately (§2.3…

audit.reasoning: The classification rests on the standard and only reference grammar (Musgrave 2007, PL 587), held as an open ANU PDF; the deciding quotation and the author's stress marks were re-verified on the rendered page (PDF p.31 = p.21, ex. 2.46-2.48), and the supporting syllable-structure and domain quotes were found at the stated sections. The older secondary (Crowley 2002 sketch) agrees on penultimate stress. noted). The 'weight (final CVV)' reading is an analytic consequence of Musgrave's tautosyllabic VV plus her -VV(C) rule and is already documented in the record with the plain-penult alternative from Crowley; nothing found suggests reclassification. list of works to obtain holds only two low-priority comparative Lynch papers.
